The Value of Dharma as a Means to Liberation (mokṣa)
Having prostrated before the Supreme Self, I shall, out of a desire for the welfare of beings of limited intelligence, set forth the *Śāstravārttāsamuccaya*.
Having heard which, for the most part, a definitive determination of reality arises regarding all treatises;
it pacifies hatred and brings about the happiness of heavenly success.
"Suffering arises from evil and happiness from dharma; this is established in all scriptures.
Therefore, one should not commit evil, but should accumulate dharma. (HSvs 1.1.3)
Violence, falsehood, and the other [three], lack of faith in the principles, and the four beginning with anger—these are the causes of evil. (HSvs 1.1.4)
But these very same things are declared by the Buddhas to be the opposites of the Dharma;
one who desires happiness should always exert effort correctly regarding them.
Constant service to the virtuous with devotion, friendliness toward all beings from the heart, and the relinquishing of grasping at "mine" are the means for accomplishing the causes of the Dharma.
Constantly receiving auspicious instruction and seeing those who practice the Dharma,
as well as discipline in the proper place— this is the great fruit of serving the virtuous.
For one who constantly cultivates loving-kindness, a virtuous disposition arises;
from the emergence of that disposition, the fire of hatred in a living being is extinguished.
By relinquishing the grasping at "mine," even craving— which gives rise to every fault and destroys every virtue— is brought to cessation.
Thus, one endowed with a multitude of virtues, pure in soul, and firm in resolve,
is declared to be a knower of reality and a true practitioner of the Dharma.
And it is the pure Dharma alone that the Buddhas always regard as what is to be adopted within cyclic existence for the sake of liberation; for everything else is a cause of suffering.
Union with loved ones in this world is impermanent, fraught with envy, grief, and attachment;
and youth, too, is impermanent, being the locus for contemptible conduct.
Prosperities are impermanent, arising from a multitude of intense afflictions;
likewise, life here is impermanent, as is the bondage to all conditioned phenomena.
There is rebirth and repeated death, and taking refuge in inferior and other such states;
because of this constant recurrence, no happiness is found here.
For everything in this cyclic existence is indeed beautiful only by its very nature;
therefore, tell me, what basis for attachment could there be here for those who possess discernment?

Having abandoned the Dharma—which is venerable by the world, stainless, eternal, the accomplisher of the welfare of others, and practiced by the wise who are rich in virtuous conduct— [one follows what is contrary]. 1.16.16.
He said: Even in that case, it is not logical if one examines it correctly;
for even the auspicious dharma is considered to have bondage itself as its fruit.
And at that time, there is no difference whatsoever between the fruit of an iron bond and one made of gold, because there is no difference in their state of dependence.
Therefore, just like unrighteousness (*adharma*), righteousness (*dharma*) must likewise be abandoned by those seeking liberation,
since liberation has been described by the sages as resulting from the exhaustion of both dharma and adharma.
It is said: it is exactly so; however, Dharma is considered to be twofold:
one is the application of correct cognition, and the other is characterized by merit.
The yoga of knowledge is pure austerity, free from the defect of longing;
it is declared that through the excellence of practice, this is the means for achieving liberation.
If those dharmas are also true, why does that [other person] not have the fruit of bondage?
Why is it not the same for another who is free from longing? If you say it is not so, it is because it is not so.

Dharma has enjoyment and liberation as its fruits; it consists of both active engagement and its opposite, and takes the form of the correct, the false, and so forth—this is also taught in other tantras.
But without that [cause], by what means could the destruction of those two be established?
For if it were indeed causeless, it would either exist at all times or never at all.
Therefore, some cause for the destruction of those two must necessarily be admitted;
that very factor is to be known as the pure dharma that bestows the fruit of liberation.

Liberation results from the exhaustion of both merit and demerit; and as for that which is described as having the characteristic of merit, it is the dharma that is to be abandoned by relying upon it, and not the application of conceptual cognition.
Therefore, if one investigates correctly, it is precisely therein that one should apply oneself;
for everything else in cyclic existence has been shown to be a cause of suffering.
And how liberation arises from that, being free from death and the like,
we shall explain further below in accordance with the authentic scriptures.

Now, however, the correctness of the treatise is stated in brief: by way of being free from contradiction through the refutation of the faulty arguments and misinterpretations of those who propound erroneous doctrines. (HSvs 1.1.29)
(2) Refutation of the Doctrine of Elemental Consciousness:
This world is merely the effect of the great elements, such as earth and the rest; the proponents of the elements do not believe in the existence of a self or a seer. (HSvs 1.2.30)
Others maintain that the primary elements are insentient; they possess neither that property [of sentience] nor its fruit. Rather, he who possesses this sentience is the self.
If this [nature] were an inherent property of those [elements], it would be perceived in each of them at all times,
just as [properties such as] existence or solidity are.
Because it always exists within them in the form of a potentiality (śakti), it is not perceived;
yet, if it were truly non-existent even in that form, it would not be so.
Whether there be identity or difference between the power and its possessor in every respect:
if they are identical, that [power] is just consciousness itself; if they are different, then that [power] belongs to another.
Furthermore, its non-manifestation is not logically tenable, because an obscuration by something else would contradict the established enumeration of the principles (*tattva*). (HSvs 1.2.35)
And that [manifestor] does not exist either in its own form or as one of those [sounds], because it is asserted to be a manifestor; for that which is unmanifested cannot be a manifestor.
For even when there is no distinct transformation, there is indeed no obscuration here;
because existence is perceived, it would otherwise follow that the name itself is the manifestor. (HSvs 1.2.37)

And this [universal] is not distinct from the primary elements (*bhūta*), for if it were, manifestation would occur at all times. If there were a difference, however, the enumeration of the principles (*tattva*) would be untenable due to the addition of further entities.
"Unbroken in its own time"—this [definition] is not tenable in the absence of time.
Alas! If one relies on what is established by worldly consensus, why is the self (*ātman*) not accepted? (HSvs 1.2.39)
Nor is a self established in the world, because of the reliance on the recollection of past births;
and for all [beings], its absence exists due to the ripening of diverse karma.
In the world as well, it is not observed that for all those who have come from various different places,
there is a recollection of experienced objects without distinction.
Moreover, because of divine vision, because of the non-deviation of their remnants,
and because of the accomplishment of ancestral rites (*pitṛkarma*) and so forth— alas! even the self (*ātman*) is not something beyond the world (*alaukika*).
The elements, being of the nature of solidity and non-cognition, are established by direct perception;
but consciousness is not of that nature—how then could it be their effect?
If it were non-existent in each of those [atoms], it would not exist [in the aggregate], like oil in sand;
if it were existent, it would be perceived at all times within things that have distinct forms.

If it is thought that just as grossness—which is non-existent—is perceived in atoms and the like, or in jars and the like, so too consciousness exists within the elements even though it is non-existent; [then this is the view].
Bulk does not exist in atoms and the like, because it arises from those very [atoms];
the production of something non-existent from them is not logical, as it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Since the fifth element would likewise arise from those [four], as there is no difference in its lack of existence, the enumeration of the principles (tattva-saṃkhyā) would not be tenable.
If those [atoms] do not have the nature of producing that [gross object], then there is no evidence for them in this case;
if the production of grossness is accepted, then that [evidence] is equally present even when those [atoms] exist.
And this [notion] that "grossness" is something distinct from an aggregate of material atoms is not tenable;
rather, it is logical that those very atoms exist in such a state, since this does not contradict valid means of knowledge.
If it were distinct [from its parts], how could it attain existence?
For if it existed even in the absence of those [parts], it would either exist eternally or everywhere.
Nor is consciousness accepted as being merely the aggregate of the elements;
for, in the absence of any distinction, it would follow that consciousness exists everywhere, just like those elements.

This being the case, because jars and other such things possess manifest consciousness, they would have no distinction from the *puruṣa*; and that [absence of distinction] is contradicted by direct perception.
Furthermore, since the primary elements themselves possess distinct intrinsic natures, it is also incorrect to claim that consciousness exists within their aggregates. (HSvs 1.2.53)

When [the elements] consist of nothing but the primary elements (*bhūta*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not differ according to reason; for without a qualifier, there can be no distinction among things that are equal. (HSvs 1.2.54)
If there is a difference consisting merely of the difference in essential nature, then the difference would be of the nature of being either an entity or its opposite;
however, if there were a separate factor effecting that difference, it would follow that that very factor is the self.

If it is argued that even those things produced from a collection of substances, such as sacrificial offerings consisting of molasses, grains, and so forth, are like edible delicacies which possess distinct individual natures; [then the following applies].
Surely, these [entities] possess distinct natures merely by virtue of being individuals;
yet no difference is observed in their effects, such as taste, potency, or post-digestive transformation.

If it were merely the state of having that as its essence, then why is it not the case that this [cognition] exists for beings just as this [external object], which is distinct from configuration and so forth, does? (HSvs 1.2.58)

Because there is no agent, and because distinctions such as space and time are incompatible [with it], this [reason] is not unestablished; for if [the world] were merely the primary elements (*bhūtamātra*), such [distinctions] would be impossible. (HSvs 1.2.59)

And likewise, if there were only the elements, no distinction between their combination and their dissolution would be logical due to the absence of any differentiating factor; let this be properly considered. (HSvs 1.2.60)
"One is thus and the other is not"—if [the difference] were merely that much, then it would be of such a kind;
since even that is not distinct [from them], therefore it is equal for both of them.

It might be argued that even though stones and such things are derived from the primary elements (*bhūta*), their diversity is established by worldly consensus; thus, it is already established that this [diversity] is not produced from those [elements] alone. (HSvs 1.2.62)
Because [cognition] arises from a causal complex including unperceived space, time, and so forth, it is understood by worldly convention in that very way; otherwise, it would not exist.
Nor is the worldly path being examined by us here;
rather, we have stated that it is not tenable within your own system, as to where it might possibly be applicable.
Furthermore, consciousness would be perceived in every way within a dead body;
for it exists as a property of the body and so forth, and not otherwise.
Nor is there any deviation [of the reason] due to beauty, hardness, or darkness,
because these are observed to exist even in a dead body through direct perception itself.
If the existence of beauty does not have that [body] alone as its cause, then for this very reason—because of the existence of something else—it is established that the self exists. (HSvs 1.2.67)
Breath and so forth are not the means of valid cognition for that [self]; why then is there equality [of their presence] even when that [self] is present?
If it is argued that [the self is known] because of its absence when they are absent, then what proof is there for the existence of the self when it is not perceived?
Therefore, its occurrence through that [specific cause] is no longer established by means of a tube or similar devices;
for even if such [artificial] means were employed, this [result] would still be achieved, and thus it would not be distinct from the other. If you say this, it is not so.

If it is argued that this [cognition] of yours does not [establish the object] because of doubt regarding that very [object],
then how can there be an absence of that [object], given its existence in its own respective nature?

Because there is a cognition of its distinctness from that [self], this [error] would not be a defect in the case of a son born from the consciousness of the mother; nor would it be a defect if the mother herself were non-existent.
And that [consciousness] cannot exist as the mother-substance in beings born from moisture and so forth;
furthermore, even the example of the lamp does not constitute a refutation here, because it serves merely as a causal condition.
Thus, its being an appropriation is not tenable in any way;
moreover, if it were to have another as its appropriation, it would follow that it is itself the self.
Nothing arises without a cause that brings it about in such a manner, nor does anything perish absolutely; as the great seer Vyāsa has said.
The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being.
The limit of both these is seen by the seers of reality.
Non-existence does not become existence, as is known from the case of a rabbit’s horn;
nor does existence here become non-existence, for if a lamp were not [subject to change], it would not cease in any way whatsoever.
Thus, the self is established as possessing consciousness by virtue of its constant existence;
it should also be understood as existing in the next world by those who follow the path of reasoning.
(3) [Objection: Is there not a perception of this self through the direct experience of objects, just as there is of a jar? [Reply:
There certainly is a clear perception, because it is known through the cognition of the "I"-notion (*ahaṃpratyaya*). (HSvs 1.3.79)

"I am deluded; this one is the teacher"—this is true, but that other person is considered [the teacher] because of his non-deviation; otherwise, it might be argued that this [deluded person] lacks the capacity to convey [knowledge]. (HSvs 1.3.80)
Even that which is perceptual must be abandoned because there is no difference in its actual existence;
if the other [type of cognition] is a pseudo-perception, then it is not valid, as it is subject to deviation.
Even on the side of the view that the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) [is the self], surely all this is the same;
therefore, like that [other cognition], it should be accepted as a primary and correct perception (samyak-pratyakṣa).

Because a cognition of difference is observed in such cases as "My body is heavy," it is logical that this [cognition of identity] belongs only to what is considered erroneous, and not to any other [valid cognition].
Even the grasping of a self by the self is established for him through such experience;
because that very [self] has that nature, it is not, however, logically untenable.
Nor can this ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) be conceived as a specific kind of cognition, because it is experienced as "I" even at the time of cognitions such as giving and so forth. (HSvs 1.3.85)
When the self is grasped by the self, because of its connection with that very nature,
it must be understood that there is always non-apprehension due to the defect of karma.
Therefore, this self is established by direct perception for all living beings as being eternally self-luminous; likewise, it is recited in the Veda as well.
(4) Regarding the self and likewise regarding karma, some wise Buddhists here also describe a different opinion:
"There exists a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) which is eternal, and it possesses the characteristics of the self as previously described. [HSvs 1.4.88]
If it is eternal, then it is the self itself; here there is merely a difference in terminology.
But if it is non-eternal, then this does not possess the characteristics of the self as previously described.
He who is the agent of various actions and the enjoyer of the fruit of those actions,
who transmigrates and attains final nirvana— he indeed is the self, and not anything else characterized by different marks.

The diversity of that [Self], which is indistinguishable in its nature as a Self, by virtue of which it takes on forms such as human and so forth— that manifold [principle] is called *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen), also known as *karman* (action).
Likewise, even when the undertaking is equal and the means are virtuous, that difference in the results among men which occurs would not be logical for us without some other cause.
Therefore, others must necessarily accept another cause in that case; those who have exerted themselves in the study of the scriptures call that very thing "the unseen" (adṛṣṭa).
Because the elements possess that nature, the claim "this [self] exists" is also not a valid answer;
for it has been demonstrated here that the self is not of the very nature of the elements.
Or rather, this [karma] is also currently considered to be material;
for it is regarded as being distinct from the self and possessing a variegated nature.
Other wise ones, however, declare that it is of the nature of a potency (śakti);
others, moreover, consider it to be of the nature of a latent impression (vāsanā), which yields diverse fruits.
But others assert here: "How can there be an accidental power for an agent who is restricted by his own nature, in the absence of a connection with something else? [HSvs 1.4.97]
If that [growth] occurs through connection with its activity, it is not logical if there is no nourishment of it;
and in the absence of connection with anything else, how could its growth occur? (HSvs 1.4.98)
That [power] certainly exists always, but it is manifested only through the act of desiring;
for one who remains in the state of the Self alone, there is never any manifestation of it.

Because there is no other obscuration [to it], or because this very [cognition] is its object; since manifestation occurs through the removal of that [obscuration], the establishment of its distinction [from others] follows from that.
Let that [result] be distinct from the action itself, being the basis for another action;
likewise, why is merit not seen as being produced by a desired action?

Even a latent impression (vāsanā) is not possible without a connection to something else, since it is not observed in sesame seeds and the like when the fragrance of flowers and such is absent. (HSvs 1.4.102)
Let some primary perfuming agent be accepted as something distinct from mere cognition;
for that alone is [properly] your "action," otherwise perfuming is not tenable.
If that [nature] were present in mere consciousness, there would be no knowledge free from latent impressions;
consequently, there would always be a lack of liberation, for there is no distinction in pure [consciousness] alone.
Thus, this position regarding [the existence of] power (*śakti*) and so forth does not hold up logically;
for, due to the deficiency or excess of bondage, its existence is not established by reason. (HSvs 1.4.105)
Therefore, that which is distinct from its own self, yet real, variegated, and connected to the self,
must be understood as the unperceived [adṛṣṭa], which establishes its powers and so forth.
The unseen force (adṛṣṭa), karma, formative predispositions (saṃskāra), merit and demerit,
the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as dharma and adharma— these are proclaimed to be synonyms for that "bond" (pāśa).
For its causes have been previously declared as violence, falsehood, and so forth;
one who possesses those [causes] becomes joined with that [karma] which yields various fruits.
Since there is no contradiction with what is seen or what is accepted, and since its establishment remains unimpeded,
the wise declare this alone to be the doctrine of reality (tattvavāda).
(5) Conclusion of the Refutation of the Theory of Material Consciousness:
The wise should know that the Lokāyata doctrine is a cause for a flood of evils;
since it thus runs contrary to reality, it does not increase knowledge. (HSvs 1.5.110)
It is said that Bṛhaspati devised this for the purpose of deceiving Indra;
yet even that is devoid of logic, since Indra would not be deceived in such a manner.
Therefore, the wise should always avoid the nihilistic view, which corrupts the disposition, is conceived by afflicted beings, and consists of evil teachings.
Second Chapter (2): Some Questions Concerning Merit, Demerit, and Liberation.
Unwholesome karma arises from violence and other such acts; wholesome karma arises from those other than these.
Nor do others say, "From what source does this restriction arise from the means of knowledge? [HSvs 2.1.113]

But others, however, maintain that [the means of knowledge] other than those [perception and inference] is called scripture (*āgama*); and that [scripture] is uncontradicted by what is seen and so forth, has all things as its object, is eternal, and its meaning is made manifest by the Supreme Self.
Therefore, because agreement with reality is observed in cases such as eclipses of the moon and sun,
it is not tenable to deny its validity even regarding things that are imperceptible, such as demerit (*pāpa*).
Even if a correspondence were observed in some other object,
how could its existence or its true nature be determined?
And that [authoritativeness] is established through the unity of the tradition (āgama), by means of the similarity of its sentences and so forth,
through a well-established lineage of transmission, and likewise through the destruction of evil.
Otherwise, the very examination of the true nature of reality would not be tenable,
because doubt arises everywhere for one who is still under the veil of ignorance.
Even non-examination is not appropriate for us, because it fails to distinguish between virtues and faults;
I fear that a great peril has come upon the proponent of logic.

Therefore, from the aforementioned valid means of knowledge known as authoritative scripture, this restriction is established: that from acts such as violence, [results] such as unwholesomeness [arise].
From the performance of afflicted acts such as violence, there is the acquisition of afflicted karma;
just as for one who eats unwholesome food, whereas from the opposite [practice], there is the acquisition of non-afflicted [karma], like [the recovery] from disease.
This is the very nature of the soul:
that it undergoes such transformation as to be bound by merit and demerit, yet it is liberated through equanimity.
Even after traveling very far and establishing numerous arguments here,
who would not finally take refuge in intrinsic nature and scripture?
Since these two are sublated by the nature of their antidotes and by the arrival of those antidotes, how can they possibly serve as a refuge for those who speak according to reason?
Whatever is sublated by its dependence [on conditions], that intrinsic nature is not tenable,
even when it is imagined for a thing— just as coldness and the like are not tenable for fire and so forth.
Fire certainly possesses coldness; why is its effect not seen?
For it is indeed seen when near snow; how can this be so by way of intrinsic nature?
This is the very nature of snow that it invariably causes burning when in proximity to fire; likewise, why should fire and the like not possess coldness?

For indeed, because there is no fixed distinction, this cognition of yours regarding this [object] is such that whatever effect it has upon a clod of earth, that same effect would come from you, owing to your having that same nature.
In this way, the emptiness of cognition would follow for you as well.
If that were so, what dispute could we have with one who is entirely devoid of cognition?

But another says here: "Even if it is established that [results] such as suffering arise from non-virtuous actions such as violence, by what means of valid cognition is it understood that happiness and so forth arise specifically from virtuous actions?"
On this point also, some who argue entirely from reason state:
"This is indeed determined by means of reasoning that has perception as its core. (HSvs 2.1.131)
Therefore, they say that happiness does not arise from the unwholesome, because that would entail the consequence of its abundance;
for those who perform evil deeds are many, while those who perform wholesome deeds are few.
And this is not seen in the world, because we observe an abundance of suffering;
happiness results from the wholesome, and therefore it is established that [the cause] is other than that, and likewise [the effect] is other than that.
Furthermore, other faithful ones declare this according to scripture:
"It is from virtue and so forth alone that happiness and so forth are understood, and never from anything else. (HSvs 2.1.134)
Regarding entities that are beyond the senses and of such a nature,
there generally exists no non-erroneous means of valid cognition for one who is still under the veil of ignorance (chadmastha).
And as for what was said regarding the observation of an abundance of suffering, that is not a proof; for even if it is observed in some instances, it is not seen everywhere.
If one has perception of everything [through inference], why is that [inference] not a means of proof?
It is indeed a means of proof; thus, it does not differ from scripture (āgama).
And whatever attainment of happiness occurs anywhere even from the performance of an impure act,
that fruit is the bitter ripening of such a deed.
Just as one obtains a village or similar reward by carrying out an instruction for the killing of a Brahmin,
this [result] is not understood from that very [act] alone, but rather from the scriptural injunction itself.
Furthermore, because the scriptures of opposing schools contradict both what is perceived and what is accepted,
and because they were composed by those who are not authoritative, it is not logical for them to possess the status of scripture.
Furthermore, because they contradict both what is perceived and what is accepted, it is understood that they were not composed by a reliable authority;
since this is established through necessity, it is precisely this [necessity] that is being demonstrated.

The claim that engaging in sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached and so forth constitutes a means for accomplishing the Dharma contradicts direct perception as it is commonly established in the world.
Liberation is likewise held to arise precisely from the excellence of one's own dharma;
that its existence [should occur] due to the absence of a cause is contradicted by what is accepted [as a necessary condition].

Neutrality itself is the cause of that [liberation]; since it is established by means of such things as approaching those who should not be approached, there is no fault whatsoever in that supreme state.
This too is a mere assertion: that because one engages in such acts as approaching those who should not be approached, neutrality cannot be established through reasoning.

Because of the practice of pure cultivation, there arises that supreme equanimity, which results from the non-occurrence [of conceptualization] everywhere due to the presence of one's capacity as it is.
As long as such activity does not proceed in this manner, so long is that [activity] excellent without distinction; for this establishes its superiority.
This [non-perception] is not a cause for non-occurrence, because there is no cessation from anything;
since existence is uninterrupted everywhere, otherwise there would be an established state of what is to be understood.
And let that which is taught in the worldly scriptures be so, because of the resulting state of indifference;
for this supreme [state] is possible for great-souled ones due to the purity of their disposition.
For even for the one who liberates [beings] from saṃsāra, violence is a means to dharma;
since liberation exists through that [violence], this fault remains unavoidable for him as well.
Liberation arises solely from the exhaustion of karma and never from anything else;
since that [liberation] is devoid of birth and so forth, it is precisely that which is being defined here.
Is that destruction of karma indeed accomplished through the excellence of violence and so forth, or born from its opposite, or caused by something else, or even causeless? [HSvs 2.1.152]
If [liberation] were to be accomplished by the excellence of violence and so forth, then in the absence of those, it would not exist;
and if there were no stability in the destruction of karma, the liberation of those already liberated would perish.
If it were to be established as the opposite of that, it would result in the acceptance of the opponent's own tenets;
for, according to the virtuous, the destruction of karma is accomplished through non-violence and other such means.
If it were to be produced by causes other than that [nature], its own nature would not be established;
if it were causeless, it would indeed always exist or always be non-existent.
Liberation is held to result from the destruction of karma, and that [destruction] is the fruit of the yoga of knowledge;
furthermore, non-violence and so forth are its causes—this is the principle esteemed by the virtuous.
Thus, even violence prescribed by the Vedas leads to ruin in reality,
because it is sublated by other scriptural statements, despite its being enjoined by the treatises.

One should not harm living beings in this world; harming is considered to produce fault, as is clear from the medical treatises (*vaidyaka*) regarding the prohibition of burning, which is a general rule of exception.
Therefore, when an injunction is issued, burning [the body] must be performed for the sake of curing the disease;
even so, there would be no fault, because the injunction is made with a specific result in view.
Thus, even regarding the existence of that result, since it is enjoined by scripture,
a fault necessarily arises in every respect from the injunction of the result.
In the same way, the contradiction of other false treatises with both what is perceived and what is accepted must be demonstrated through reasoning alone;
therefore, this [point] is established.
For if the performance of afflicted acts such as violence did not arise from something else,
then that [self] alone would be the agent of every action whatsoever.
Because it is joined with beginningless karma, it proceeds from that delusion;
for the most part, even toward what is harmful to oneself, just like a mind afflicted by disease.
(1) The doctrine of time, the doctrine of inherent nature, the doctrine of necessity, and the doctrine of karma.
Other proponents maintain that time and the other factors possess agency as a causal totality;
yet others hold that they possess it individually, depending on their mutual combination.
Whatever arises in the world—such as the embryo, the infant, or auspicious events—is not produced apart from time; indeed, it is said that time is the cause of all this.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures;
Time remains awake while others sleep; for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Moreover, even the cooking of mung beans is not admitted to occur without time, despite the presence of the pot and other factors; therefore, this [cooking] is held to depend upon time.
Furthermore, in the absence of time, everything beginning with conception would occur without any fixed order,
because that [conception] would arise solely from the mere presence of the causes desired by the opponent.
Whatever arises in the world—whether it be an embryo, an infant, or something auspicious—is not produced apart from its own intrinsic nature; indeed, that [nature] is said to be the cause.
All phenomena, by their own intrinsic nature, proceed and likewise cease within their respective natures, turning away from the practice of acting according to desire.
In this world, even the cooking of mung beans is not admitted to exist by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
because such cooking does not occur for horse-gram even when the conditions of time and so forth are present.
If something were to exist despite not having that nature, an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would be unavoidable.
In that case, it would be irrational to say that from clay only a jar arises and not a cloth or other things, since [the lack of their nature] is equal in both instances. (HSvs 2.2.172)
Since all things exist only in a fixed form,
they are born of necessity (niyati), because they are permeated by that very nature.

Whenever, from whatever source, and to whatever extent something arises, at that very time, from that very source, and in that very manner, it necessarily arises by virtue of logical necessity; who is capable of subverting this?
One cannot even observe the ripening of mung beans as being subject to no fixed order in this world;
for even when their intrinsic nature and other conditions are present, that ripening is not indeterminate.
Otherwise, it would follow that all things are indeterminate;
furthermore, because they would result in being identical with one another's natures, there would be a total futility of action.
In this world, there is no object of enjoyment apart from an enjoyer;
nor can there be enjoyment for that which has not been created, because liberated beings are devoid of enjoyment.
And whatever is perceived as an object of experience for sentient beings through this or that specific method—all this is indeed directly perceived; therefore, it is certainly born of karma.

Furthermore, even the cooking of mung beans is not observed when there is a deficiency in the action [of cooking], such that it does not occur in some cases due to the breaking of the pot or other factors. (HSvs 2.2.179)
The diversity of experience likewise arises from diverse karma; otherwise, it would lack a cause.
For its manifold variety cannot be logically accounted for by necessity (*niyati*) or other such factors.
Because destiny has a fixed nature, there would be uniformity among destined things;
likewise, if they were of an undetermined nature, their diversity would necessarily arise by force.
Furthermore, its diversity is not tenable if it arises from mere existence and so forth,
unless there is a differentiator other than those, in accordance with correct reasoning and without contradiction.
The diversity of water, though uniform in its own nature, does not arise from falling into the sky unless there is a differentiation in the earth, such as saline soil and the like.
And if it were the differentiator of that which is distinct from it, it would not be its agent;
yet if it were its agent, its variegated nature—and likewise that [of the object]—would be equally untenable.
If it is maintained that its very nature is of such a kind,
then surely the doctrine of necessity (niyativāda) would be abandoned, since one would instead be relying upon intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
And intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed one's own being (*svasattā*), for it exists as such by its very nature;
yet, in the absence of any differentiator for that [nature], diversity is not logically possible.
Consequently, because that [cause] would be indistinguishable [from others], the simultaneous arising of the entire universe would follow;
and since this is not the case, the doctrine [of such a cause] is not tenable through sound reasoning.
If that cause of the universe depends upon various factors such as time and so forth,
then surely it would be a doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda), since it would be adopting [the role of] time.
Time as well, beginning with the [specific] occasion (*samaya*) and so forth, is also a cause;
for it is precisely because of that [time] that the non-arising of anything is not possible.
And therefore, even when the time is equal, that result does not occur everywhere;
hence, the wise should understand that it depends upon other causes.
Therefore, all factors such as time and the rest should be understood by proponents of reason as the cause of the entire collection of effects, such as the embryo, through their collective operation.
And nowhere here is anything observed to arise from a single cause alone;
therefore, it is held that the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is the producer of every effect.
Others declare that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and necessity (*niyati*) are distinct from action (*karman*); yet others [declare them] as the two properties of every entity in its general aspect.
The Third Chapter (1): Refutation of the Doctrine of God. Some here maintain that God is the agent by virtue of being the impeller.
He is endowed with inconceivable, supreme power, and is primordially pure, according to the wise.
The Lord of the World possesses a fourfold set of qualities that are innate: unimpeded knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and righteousness.
This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into the abyss.
Others, however, state here: "Since one who is free from passion is thus devoid of purpose in reality, how can agency be appropriate for him? [HSvs 3.1.197]
For what reason does he swiftly impel certain beings toward actions that result in hell and the like, while impelling others toward actions that achieve heaven and the like?
If sentient beings proceed spontaneously toward artistic works,
how can the agency of a Lord in this world be said to be purposeless?
If it bestows all results, then everything here is impelled by that [Brahman];
if it were resultless, the aforementioned fault would apply, but if it possesses results, it would be nothing more than devotion.

Even at the time of the initial creation, no cause exists for that which has already accomplished its purpose, because that would contradict the initial proposition; furthermore, an inherent nature (svabhāva) is also devoid of any means of valid cognition.
If that nature [of omniscience] were identical to karma and so forth, nothing would be contradicted for the All-pervading One;
however, if the All-pervading One were of that nature, it would contradict his state of having already accomplished all that was to be done.
Therefore, this doctrine of God as the creator is ultimately tenable,
provided it is consistent with correct reasoning, as those of pure intellect have stated.
The Lord is indeed the Supreme Self; because liberation results from the practice of the vows prescribed by Him, He is therefore its agent through His state of being the inherent quality.
Precisely because it does not practice that [action], even though cyclic existence exists in reality,
there is no fault in postulating its agency as well.
Since some people have respect for the statement "this is the creator," the teaching of his status as a creator is given in accordance with that [view]. (HSvs 3.1.206)
Because he possesses supreme sovereignty, the Self alone is considered the Lord;
and since He is the agent, the doctrine of agency is established as being faultless.
The great-souled authors of the treatises are for the most part free from craving for existence and are dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings; how could they speak what is improper?

Therefore, one who desires their welfare should correctly investigate their intention in a manner that does not contradict the treatises on logic, just as Manu has also said this: [The verse continues: "One should not, out of devotion to the Vedas, cause a learned Brahmin to abandon his own duty; for he who abandons his own duty and follows another's path falls from both worlds. He who investigates the teachings of the sages and the treatises on Dharma with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows Dharma; no one else does.
(2) Refutation of the Doctrine of Primordial Matter and the Spirit:
However, other wise men believe that everything here indeed arises from Pradhāna (primordial matter) through the sequence beginning with Mahat (the Great One). [HSvs_3.2.211]
From Pradhāna arises Mahat; from that, Ahaṃkāra;
from that, the group of the senses and the subtle elements (tanmātras); and from the subtle elements, the collection of gross elements.
Even objects such as jars arise from the transformation of earth and other elements;
not even one among them is found in the world to be produced by the activity of a self.
But others say this is merely a description of the process;
without investigating it through reasoning, the supreme [reality] is understood through faith alone.
Since the Pradhāna is held to be eternal by means of reasoning,
how could Mahat and the other evolutes come into being if it were not to deviate from that very state?
If it is argued that this is because that very thing has that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why does it not exist at all times?
If it is argued that it is for this very reason, then if it is of such a nature, from where indeed does that [nature] arise?
Without being the substrate of another, one thing can never exist as something else;
and if it were its substrate, that [substrate] could not be absolutely eternal.
Even objects such as jars are seen by you to depend upon potters and the like;
therefore, they do not arise from the transformation of earth and other elements.
Even in that case, if the body were the agent, it would not be distinct from the self;
if, on the other hand, it were indeed distinct, how could experience be attributed to the self?
In reality, no enjoyment of this [deity] through the body and its enjoyments is intended;
rather, it is through the arising of a reflection, as has been stated by the ancient masters.

“The person, whose nature is indeed unchanging, causes the insentient mind—which bears his own reflection—to act through mere proximity, just as an adjunct causes a crystal [to appear colored]. (HSvs 3.2.221)
"Experience (bhoga) is said to belong to this [Self] when the intellect has undergone a transformation into a distinct form of perception;
it is like the reflection of the moon arising in clear water. [HSvs 3.2.222]
Even the arising of a reflection for this [consciousness] is not tenable by virtue of its being formless;
furthermore, because of the over-extension [of such a view], there would never be any experience for those who are liberated.
Furthermore, because it possesses its prior nature, that [transformation] is inconsistent for those who are liberated;
and if there were the existence of another nature, transformation would be unavoidable.
If this [self] were indeed distinct from the body, then acts such as violence could never occur;
since those [acts] would be absent, being without a cause, how could there be auspicious or inauspicious bondage?
Without bondage, neither saṃsāra nor liberation is possible for this [being];
and in the absence of that [bondage], everything beginning with the restraints (yama) is indeed purposeless.
The self is never bound, nor is it ever liberated;
if it is argued that it is rather *prakṛti* itself that is bound and liberated within its own nature, [then the following applies].

For that [nature] which is exclusively of one form and eternal, bondage and liberation are not possible in every respect, because there is no other activity for it; however, they are logically possible [only if it is otherwise].
Liberation is the dissociation from primordial nature (prakṛti); therefore, how could that [liberation] belong to this [Self]?
For it would entail the loss of its own essential nature, and furthermore, it would contradict the Tantras.
One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot—is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
"The liberation of the person has been declared in the Tantra by the ancients;
if this were not possible, then everything would be illogical. (HSvs 3.2.231)
In this regard as well, other disputants desire liberation for the person (puruṣa),
and they also [assert it] for primordial matter (prakṛti) through reasoning, as well as for the nature of karma itself.
And because that [consciousness] possesses manifold forms, is subject to transformation,
and constitutes a bondage for the self, the aforementioned faults do not arise.
The formless does not attain form, nor does the formed attain formlessness;
for by whatever bond and by whatever logic, the self remains unconnected with it.
"It does not go away at all because of the perception of touch on the body and so forth"—this is an exaggeration.
Since this [perception] arises from mutual pervasion, bondage and the like are logically consistent.
Just as the self, though possessing form, can have a connection with space,
so too can it undergo states such as injury, just as consciousness does through liquor and the like.
In this way, the doctrine of primordial nature (prakṛti) should also be understood as truly real;
for it was spoken by Kapila, and he was indeed a divine great sage.
Others consider the entire world to be bound by afflictions and karma; [this is the introduction to the refutation of the doctrine of momentariness].
Others [hold that] great wisdom perishes moment by moment, and likewise that it is merely cognition.
They say that everything is momentary because a cause for destruction is impossible,
because of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because of transformation, and because decay is observed.
And whatever in the world is mere cognition is experienced as cognition alone;
there is no object apart from that [cognition], and therefore that [object] does not exist at all.

Regarding this, others also state: "Because recollection and so forth would be impossible, and because of the cognition of external objects, all of this [the aforementioned arguments] is pointless. (HSvs_4.1.241)
Since worldly recollection has as its object an entity previously experienced,
it is not tenable for this [recollection] to be primary [i.e., eternal] if that object were impermanent over time.
Thus, the disciple and the teacher are recognized as being non-identical;
there is the observation of curiosity, agitation, engagement, and indeed attainment.
For the experience of one's own actions is indeed cast far away;
for that very cause which is the practice of ethical discipline perishes at that same moment.
All our conventional usage is held to depend upon the continuum;
and since that [continuum] is indeed one, why is it not tenable?
In whichever very continuum the latent impression of karma has been deposited,
therein alone does it bear fruit, just as redness [appears] in cotton.

This too is a mere assertion; for one who maintains that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause, it is illogical that there should be a distinct continuum [of the self] by way of the relationship between cause and effect.
(2) Refutation of the view that existence becomes non-existence:
"Non-existence does not become existence, because it is like the horn of a hare;
likewise, existence here does not become non-existence, due to such faults as its [subsequent] production. (HSvs 4.2.248)
If it were non-existent while being existent, its arising would follow from that; and since its destruction follows from that, there could be no further existence for what has been destroyed.
Destruction would be eternal, and not the persistence of that [entity].
If that [entity] has the property of existing for only a single moment, then its existence in a second or subsequent moment would be impossible;
for this too is consistent with it, and thus there is no deviation from what has been stated.

If it were to endure for even a single moment, its non-endurance at that very time would be logically inconsistent; nor is it the case that such [non-endurance] does not occur later either. Thus, the non-existence of an existent is established.
If that [entity] does not exist, why is it not always existent? The wise know that its very non-existence is what constitutes its becoming.

Since that which is to be produced arises only occasionally, it must be non-existent [prior to its production]. But how can this be so for that which is not non-existent, given that it is indeed not non-existent? // 4.2.253 //
In that case, this [non-existence] would be equal to existence; why would it not belong to its own cessation?
Since it would have attained the state of being a mere nothingness, let it not be an entity; yet how could the non-existent be existent, or the existent-and-non-existent be both?

Since that [effect] is born from its own cause and possesses that very nature, is it not the case that this [reasoning] applies equally to the other [case] as well, because it occurs immediately after that?
Its arising does not occur without a cause, nor does it have that [non-existent thing] as its nature in the case of a void;
therefore, how could it exist? How, then, is this consistent with reason?
That very entity is its cause, because it persists in that very manner;
since its own cessation is its nature, why then is this not the case for the entity itself? // HSvs_4.257 //
Just like its being an object of knowledge, its nature as such is not illogical;
for if that [nature] were absent, there would be no cognition of it—how then could there be an understanding of its negation?

That which has such-and-such an intrinsic nature is indeed apprehended by perception in that very way; therefore, its comprehension occurs through that [perception], for there is no lack of certainty regarding this in any case.
Because it is superimposed, this [notion] is not grasped as it truly is;
however, because that [other notion] grasps it according to its actual state, it is not [the truth] either, due to the consequence of over-extension.

All this has been grasped by him; furthermore, the definitive conclusion [is reached] because of the establishment of reality through the removal of limited apprehension and superimposition. (HSvs 4.2.261)

"There is certainty regarding one thing and yet, despite an undivided experience of another, there is no such [certainty] because of a lack of vividness—this is a truly unprecedented kind of darkness. (HSvs 4.2.262)
For after the moment of its own intrinsic nature, there is emptiness due to the cessation of that [nature];
this is not correctly discerned by a cognition that apprehends only a single moment.

And as long as that [cognition] has not been apprehended, there can be no certain determination that "it is so"; for the wise do not accept that a sense faculty is a grasper of what is past and so forth.
Even prior [to the destruction], there is no perception of this [jar], because [only] the shards and so forth are perceived somewhere;
nor is that very [perception] the absence of the jar, since it is cognized as a positive entity (bhāva).
There is no movement of that [cause] into its [effect], because of the absence of any connection;
however, if it were simply non-existence, there would be continuity due to the uninterruptedness of being.
Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that what follows [the object] is indeed void;
for it is logical that this known object is known as existent even by another [cognition]. (HSvs 4.2.267)
One should understand that there is no identity between those two— non-arising and so forth— due to their distinction as being void and non-void,
as well as due to the difference in their cessation and the difference in their cognition.
By this, that which was stated by the one who fancies himself a logician is refuted:
"Nothing at all happens there; it simply does not exist. (HSvs 4.2.269)
For this conceptual distinction would exist only in the case of a positive entity (*bhāva*), since an injunction must conform to a real thing;
it has been stated that "it becomes a non-entity" (*abhāva*) just as it was said that "it becomes an entity. (HSvs 4.2.270)

By this, even in the case of causelessness, the objection regarding the faults of existence and perishability—arising from the fact that destruction occurs after having not existed—is refuted. (HSvs 4.2.271)
And that non-existence which was previously rejected— being unimpeded by the non-destruction of existence—
is at that time declared to be destructible, since it has attained the nature of a real entity (bhāva) consisting of a void.
That which is the non-becoming of an entity, and that which is the becoming of its non-existence—
in that which has such a nature, the aforementioned conceptual differentiation is not contradictory.
That very thing does not exist; this appears as if contradictory, because while it is the very thing itself, it is the negation of its existence through contact with the real entity.
Since the non-existence of an existent is thus not possible in any way, an entity does not pass into non-existence here; therefore, this is established.
(3) Refutation of the view that non-existence becomes existence:
"If there were a connection of existence with the non-existent, it would be so because of a connection with its own capacity."
It is not non-existent; yet in its absence, it is not existent, just like anything other than it.
That which arises from what is non-existent does indeed exist, provided it has a cause; and since that cause possesses specific powers, the establishment of its existence follows from that.

If everything were absolutely non-existent, it would not be logical for a cause to possess a specific capacity; indeed, such a capacity could only appear plausible if it were being postulated [within a context of existence].
That which establishes its existence is not that very thing itself at that time;
for this very reason, they should not desire this [to belong] to it, because such a connection is impossible.
In reality, that which arises immediately after something else is not different from it;
therefore, there is no purpose here for a name [that suggests otherwise].
Even without the name, without the reality, and without a specific injunction,
if it is conceived according to right reasoning, then by the very nature of things, it is so.
If [the cause] were the producer of everything, it would follow that everything exists from it;
likewise, even if one relies upon causes, its existence would not be established, just as in the case of other things.
Furthermore, that cause does not exist at the time when the effect is produced;
therefore, it cannot be its producer because of its non-existence at that time, just like something else.
Furthermore, its existence immediately [after the cause] is purposeless precisely because of its being the reality [of that cause];
and there is no connection between the destruction of the cause and the arising of the fruit, as they would be simultaneous.

Are those two [destruction and arising] distinct or non-distinct? If they are distinct from them [the entity], how could destruction and arising belong to that entity? But if there is no distinction between them, then the two would necessarily be simultaneous.
Furthermore, when that [emptiness] exists, the state of cause and effect is not tenable,
because both [cause and effect] are deprived of their basis.
If this relationship between property and substratum (dharma-dharmin) were indeed [merely] imagined in reality,
there would be no relationship of cause and effect, because that [imagined relationship] would be entirely non-existent.
The substratum (dharmin) is not conceptualized; rather, the relationship between property and substratum (dharma-dharmin-bhāva) is conceptualized.
The former [substratum] is partless, and that which follows is called the fruit.
If the prior [moment] does not exist in that manner, then alas, how could the subsequent one exist?
But if that very [prior moment] exists in that manner, then the existence of what is non-existent is not real.
The statement that "arising occurs in dependence upon that" is hollow;
it leads to an over-extension of the principle, as Mahāmati has said.
Since an effect does not arise immediately after a cause in any way whatsoever without the existence of a real entity that is destined to become such, it [the effect] does not come from the sky.
Even the perfection of imagining that very thing to have that intrinsic nature is not at all tenable,
because it is afflicted by birth through the eclipse of the lack of logical justification.
Since the status of something as an effect is established merely by its occurring immediately after that [cause],
the entire universe would be the effect of everything else, because there is no difference in their existence [immediately following one another].
Because [properties such as] non-difference of location and so forth are unestablished, because there is no positive concomitance,
and because all [such properties] are indistinguishable, they cannot be the cause for that restriction.

Even that existence of one thing [at a certain time] which is observed in a continuum at another time due to something else located in a different place— since that too arises from that very [cause], it does not constitute a contradiction.
By this, that which was stated by Sūkṣmabuddhi is refuted: "A non-existent thing cannot be an agent of becoming; nor is it [the existent] in another state. (HSvs 4.3) 296.
That existence which necessarily follows immediately after an entity is considered its effect; that very [existence] is the arising of the entity, having that [entity] as its essence.
The arising of what was non-existent is also proclaimed for this [entity] because of its prior non-existence;
it is not [an arising] through the connection of existence with the non-existent, since the effect exists by virtue of the cause.
And that [cause], having been rejected, would result in being a fruit even without a cause;
furthermore, it would entail that a non-existent entity acts as an agent, and that it undergoes a change of state.

If existence were to follow immediately after an object without that object being such [as it is], it would result either from the falling of the sky or from a connection with non-existent existence; therefore, it is not the fruit of that [object].
Nor can there be the arising of what was non-existent, precisely because it was previously non-existent;
rather, let this be properly investigated: how it is that the non-existent becomes existent.
And this [position] is not at all tenable by the logic of "non-existence as speech," because non-existence does not become existence; therefore, this [principle] is firmly established.

(4) Furthermore, even if the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) of form and so forth is postulated as the producer of cognition and the like by virtue of giving rise to a specific condition, that too is useless in the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*). HSvs_4.4 303.
If it is maintained that form and the other [sensory objects] possess the capacity to produce cognition in all [beings], then a distinction in their effects arising from them would not be logical.
A manifold effect, such as form, light, and so forth, arises from no fewer than those very [causes]; how this is so must now be considered.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to conceive of multiple [causes] as having a single capacity,
because their state of being multiple is in contradiction with that unity.
How could that which arises here dependently upon all those [causes] without exception be a single entity?
For that which has a single nature cannot exist as a plurality.
Since they possess distinct intrinsic natures, they are multiple;
and since they are produced by causal capacities, how could that [cognition] have a single form?
That which arises dependently possesses a single capacity, for it does not arise from anything else;
otherwise, because the two would result in being non-different, there would be a difference between those two as well.
Nothing whatsoever arises there through the power of a single condition;
for if it were not so, that [arising] would possess the nature of being produced from the power of all [conditions]. (HSvs 4.4.310)
For each individual instance, its possession of that nature is logical, since it possesses the aforementioned essential character;
for that universal capacity is not devoid of being present in each individual.

And it has been stated here: "Nor is the assumption that these [entities] possess that intrinsic nature (tatsvabhāvatva) sound, because it would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) and because the expression could otherwise be possible. [HSvs 4.4] 312.

If, on the other hand, a capacity for [other functions] is also attributed to form and the rest, then that very thing is not that [same thing]; thus, how can there be both multiplicity and unity in one and the same place?
Furthermore, that distinction between effects which is proclaimed on the basis of a distinction in causal complexes is also subverted by the production of diverse effects from a single [cause].
When examined through reasoning, it is not logical for a single entity to exist in the form of appropriation and so forth; therefore, the conceptualization of its unity is untenable here.

By whatever intrinsic nature form is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of form, it would be either that [same nature] or something else which serves as its efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) in cognition. (HSvs 4.4, 316)
If consciousness cannot be of the nature of cognition by that [form] alone,
then by force of another [form], it follows that form possesses a dual nature.
If it is argued that a moment of form establishes [the existence of] cognition by excluding that which does not produce cognition,
then how can a moment of form, being itself non-cognitive, establish the [existence of] form?

For indeed, although it is in reality of a single nature, it is spoken of as having a multiple nature for the sake of conventional usage, because it produces form and other qualities through its various exclusions (vyāvṛtti).
Why does this [cause] not produce smell by way of excluding the non-production of smell?
If it is argued that this is because of its absence [in the other], then it follows that there must be a positive presence of something else.
Thus, even though there is a difference in its exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), it would necessarily follow that it possesses multiple natures;
and that is untenable, because it would undermine what has been accepted.
The eyes and other sense organs possess natures that produce distinct effects;
if there were a distinction even in the resulting cognition, it would be so, but if there is no distinction, such a distinction [in their causal nature] is not tenable.
Even with respect to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this is not tenable in any way;
that which is called the "relation of cause and effect" is likewise a mere verbal expression.
(5) In the doctrine of momentariness, the relationship between the perfumer and the perfumed is untenable;
furthermore, since there is no obstruction to their distinctness, how could there be the experience of one's own actions here?
Even if this [relationship] were granted, it should be considered that because they are absolutely distinct from one another, such experience would be impossible. (HSvs_4.5) 324.
If it is argued that [the relationship between the two exists] because of the state of the perfumer and the perfumed, this is not so, because that too is impossible.
How indeed is it impossible? Because conceptual construction is untenable.
If the impression (vāsanā) were either different or non-different from the basis of impression (vāsaka), then,
if it were different, that [basis] would itself be empty of it and could not imprint anything else.
Furthermore, if it were non-different [from the substrate], there would be no transference, just as in the case of the color that perfumes;
and only when there is a substrate to be perfumed does the establishment of a portion of the substance arise.

If it were the case that [the mind] perfumes [the next moment] even in the absence of transmigration, there would be an over-extension of the principle; and such a view is outside the bounds of logic.
Furthermore, according to the principle that the relationship between the perfumer and the perfumed is not, in reality, something other than the relationship between cause and effect,
that [position] has been shown to be untenable.
(6) Regarding the impossibility of the knowledge of cause and effect within the doctrine of momentariness:
"That [cause] has the nature of producing that [effect], and likewise the produced entity is of such a nature;
therefore, because of this restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is never illogical. (HSvs 4.6) 330.

In the absence of the apprehension of both, it is not logical to postulate their existence in that manner; for you [the Yogācārins], there is no apprehension of two things by means of a single [cognition].
Just as one consciousness perceives a single object but not two consciousnesses, so too a single consciousness does not perceive two objects. (HSvs 4.6) 332
In reality, since the truth of those two is grasped by one [cognition] in that same way, it is not a sublater;
nor is there a grasping of both by one [cognition]. (HSvs 4.6.333)
Likewise, it is never logical for those two [the object and the cognition] to consist in the apprehension of one another; therefore, how could this [mutual dependence] not be a sublation?

And if there were such grasping [of the relation], how could there be a cognition of fire and so forth from the mere perception of smoke and so forth, without grasping the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) in all cases? [HSvs 4.6.335]
The claim that there is an absence of the immediately preceding [condition] in that case is untenable;
for even when two things are equal, if that [absence] were present, alas, it would not be observed in some instances.
There is no equality between those two, because for one [the cognition], the object is caused by the cause of that [cause], due to the flood [of impressions]; but it is not so for the other.

That which is the cause of the cause of the cognition that apprehends fire alone—this too is not [the object] in this way; nor is there a comprehension of it from that cognition, because its cause is not that [object].
That cognition which is not the immediate antecedent of the cognition of smoke—
because it occurred in that manner— therefore, even from that cognition, there is no apprehension of it [the fire].

If [it is argued that] "it is so" means "indeed, what is the point? It is so because of its being thus," then in the other case as well, let this cognition alone be considered as that which grasps it.

In the absence of that [present state], there is the occurrence of something else; this [change] exists for it as well. Furthermore, whether it has just passed or has been long past, it is identical in terms of its substantial reality.

By this, it should be accepted as a refutation that the cognition of smoke is produced from the cognition of fire by its very nature; thus, no other [cognition] is a producer of conceptual construction.
Therefore, since it is possible that one of the two [aspects] is not apprehended by a single [cognition],
it is not logical to postulate their existence in that way simply because they are not so perceived.

Alas, how can the relationship of cause and effect be established in this way through perception and non-perception? For that reason, it is because the existence of that [relationship] and so forth cannot be ascertained. (HSvs 4.6) 344.
In this case, the preceding and the succeeding [moments] are certainly not perceived separately from one another;
therefore, this [perception] occurs, but it is not a vision of that which transcends the senses.
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is likewise established by logic as being of that same nature, for it is not otherwise;
this is because it is produced from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of those [objects] and because it is in every respect momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
In this way, the ascertainment of that [nature] is not possible in the absence of a connection to awakening;
therefore, let this be considered by yourself, adopting a state of impartiality.
Since the cognition of fire and so forth here does not attain the status of a cognition of smoke due to a difference in form, how can there be a continuity of cognition [between them]? 4.6.348.
Through the abandonment of that form, there occurs the persistence of another form for it;
this is a consequence of cognition, which functions as a single, long-lasting determinative judgment.

Because it is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the conceptual construction that "this too is an error" is not tenable according to reason, for that would entail the consequence that everything is an error.
The determination of perishability and so forth occurs through an excessively prolonged mental engagement;
and since this [determination] is erroneous, it is not logical to say that "it is thus."
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that even some conceptual construction (vikalpa) possesses,
in some manner or other, a nature that is entirely non-erroneous (abhrānta).
While this [consciousness] exists, our [position] remains established according to the logic already stated;
for the sequence of cognitions would not arise from the production of petals [of a lotus], and because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since this [cognition], though itself of a different nature than other objects,
arises from those [objects] that are desired, there is no indubitable certainty regarding them based on it.
If there is the state of being the producer of this or that [effect], there is necessarily the connection with its own existence;
for that very thing's existence is not other than that from which the produced arises. (HSvs 4.6) 355
Thus, even though it is an entity produced by that [cause], this [nature] should be understood by the wise;
for that very thing is the entity, since it depends upon something other than itself.
Thus, the occurrence of positive concomitance arises from the very meaning of the word;
otherwise, any conceptualization of it is in every respect contradicted by logic.

That [cause], being devoid of the capacity for that form, is like any other effect; its operation is likewise non-existent, because there is no dependence on anything whatsoever due to its lack of existence.
Nevertheless, the postulation that those two alone possess that intrinsic nature is merely indicative of blindness, since the same [logical] principle applies elsewhere as well.

(7) Refutation of the doctrine of momentariness by means of the Buddha’s words: "Because of its insignificance, even the meaning of the *ārṣa* [scripture] is contradicted if [the world] were momentary; and the bringing about of such a contradiction is not the fruit of mere trifling darkness. [HSvs 4.7] 360.
"Monks, ninety-one eons ago, a man was killed by me with a spear; through the ripening of that karma, I have been pierced in the foot."
The statement "by me" is a reference to the self; the act of killing was spoken of as pertaining to that [self].
Since this was taught by the Sage himself, why do you hold to this doctrine of momentariness?
If it is argued that this was stated by the Blessed One with reference to the continuum (*saṃtāna*),
then surely that relationship of cause and effect which belongs to that [continuum] is not logically consistent with the statement "this is mine" (*tan me*).
If it is intended that the meaning of this [term "mine"] is based on the causal power [of the notion],
there is no means of valid cognition for this, because such an intention is held to be beyond the senses.
If that teaching is the means of valid cognition, it will not have any other purpose.
If one asks what the means of valid cognition is for that [teaching] as well, it is this aforementioned word of the Sage (ārṣa).
Likewise, there is another instance where the Blessed One himself, having addressed the monks, stated that the earth might in some cases endure for an eon.

"The five external [objects] are cognizable by two [kinds of cognition]"— this and other such statements of the Sage (the Buddha) are also to be understood as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establish the subject matter under discussion.
Since these [entities] are momentary, they cannot be cognized by two [cognitions];
for it is only when there is a grasping at different times that the application of those two terms and their referents is possible.
But if it were to apprehend [them] at one time, that single [cognition] would lack validity;
because it would be the grasping of what has already been grasped, the word of the Tathāgata would likewise be false.
When form and so forth have been delimited by a sense faculty, immediately thereafter,
a mental cognition arises with respect to that very same form and so forth.

And thus there is no contradiction, because of the state of being cognizable by two [consciousnesses]; yet if this applies even to the five [sense-consciousnesses] by logical principle, then this too is inconsistent.
Since even a single [atom] cannot be cognized by two [senses], because it is perceived by each one individually;
if it is argued that this is with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), no, because that would entail the existence of that [universal].
Even though [the object] exists, sensory cognition does not [perceive it]; alas, that [object] is held to be the domain [of conceptual thought].
Thus, the state of being cognizable by two [cognitions] does not truly exist when there is a difference in moments.
By this, all the proofs for momentariness have been refuted;
nevertheless, something further will be stated there specifically regarding that point as well.
Fifth Chapter:
(1) The Refutation of External Objects; the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātravāda*) is also not correctly established.
That which is pride does not exist in reality when there is an absence of any object.
It is not perception, because it is not accepted that [perception] has non-existence as its object;
nor is it inference, because no such valid logical mark (liṅga) is possible.
When an object that has reached the conditions for perception is not perceived,
its non-existence is determined by that very non-perception.
The fulfillment of the conditions for perception is the aggregation of those other causes;
if these possess that very nature, how could there be a non-establishment of it?
If it is argued that they possess the nature of producing that [cognition] by virtue of their object, then surely they must produce it;
otherwise, they would not have that nature.
Now, if you postulate that it has that nature on the basis of its fitness,
then alas, even so, [the existence of the object] is established for you at some time through perception.
Otherwise, how could their capacity [for cognition] be established by reason?
For in the world, the capacity for cooking and so forth is not established for horses, donkeys, and the like.
For if this is stated thus according to the intention of another,
it is not the case that an object which has reached the conditions for perception is perceived by him.
Even if it is not apprehended by states that do not grasp it, its non-existence does not follow from that alone, for that would lead to an over-extension.
Consciousness is that which is self-cognized, but the object is not, because it is logically untenable;
therefore, when that [consciousness] is experienced, the apprehension of the object is not established.
And thus, precisely because there is no apprehension [of it], its non-existence is determined.
Therefore, why is it said that "there is no means of valid cognition (māna) when an object is absent"? [Hs vs 5.1.385]
That which has the nature of apprehending an object is held to be self-cognizable; when that [cognition] is cognized, why is the apprehension of the [object] not thereby established? (HSvs 5.1.386)

Because there is the cognition "this is a jar" and so forth, because of the subsequent activity [toward that object], because of the attainment [of the object], because of its connection with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because of memory, and because of the occurrence of curiosity. // 387 //
If consciousness were merely cognition, it would be nothing other than cognition itself;
consequently, the activity and so forth well-established in both the world and the treatises would not exist.
Furthermore, its aversion toward the apprehension of anything other than that [cognition] would be groundless regarding the object;
for that same lack of self-awareness and so forth which occurs in the case of a different cognition would likewise apply here.
And whatever logical inconsistency regarding an object is proclaimed on account of the doctrine of universals (*jāti*),
that same [inconsistency] applies equally even in the theory of cognition (*jñānavāda*) by way of its being an apprehended object and so forth.
That [cognition] cannot have an absolute state of being the apprehended on earth due to the absence of an apprehender;
nor can it have an absolute state of being the apprehender, as that is inconsistent due to the absence of an apprehended object. (HSvs 5.1.391)
Because of contradiction, it cannot have both forms; otherwise, it would be non-existent.
Since it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), how could its existence be tenable in this way?
For consciousness is considered, in its true nature, to have illumination as its sole essence;
likewise, being devoid of an object, it illuminates itself.
Just as in such expressions as "he sits" or "he lies down," that very same [agent] is spoken of even without an object,
so too should knowledge be understood in this world.
It is said: let this now be considered by you yourself;
