for if this [existence of the self] were tenable, it would be so only due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding it.
Thus, that which [is claimed to be self-luminous] cannot even manifest itself;
therefore, this [position] is not tenable for us. Otherwise, there would be no established order.
And since the manifestation of the reality of an object as it truly exists is constant, how could that [cognition] be devoid of an object? (HSvs 5.1.397)
The establishing [cognition] of this [object] is thus erroneous in reality;
for even here, there is no non-erroneous means of valid cognition that establishes it as being "thus."
If it is argued that a distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous forms is not logically tenable—
since such a distinction is observed in the case of those with ophthalmia and the like regarding the sense organs and so forth— that is not so.
Since the cognition of defects such as those of the sense organs is itself an error— just like any other error—
if that [cognition of defects] were to exist in that same way [as an error], then for one who is erroneous, there would be non-erroneousness.
Moreover, in the world, it is not logically tenable that mere illumination—such as that of a lamp—is ever found to be without an object; therefore, this [position of yours] is pointless.
Success [in proof] cannot come from a mere example that is absolutely dissimilar in nature to the probandum;
therefore, that [example] is also nothing more than a word.

(2) The impossibility of liberation in the doctrine of consciousness-monism: Furthermore, if there is only consciousness, no distinction whatsoever exists between saṃsāra and apavarga; thus, this [doctrine] has been stated in vain. (HSvs 5.2.403)
For the mind itself, when perfumed by the afflictions such as passion and the like, is cyclic existence;
that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called the end of existence.
Since the category of afflictions such as passion is not considered distinct from consciousness,
and since that [consciousness] has an entirely uniform nature, what could be perfumed by what?
This defiled consciousness itself is that state of defilement by virtue of which it exists;
like indigo dye and so forth, this entity would consequently follow as being exactly like that [dye].
And if there were existence [of the cognition] as distinct from that [object] even in liberation, it would be like the purity of a cloth;
consequently, the undesirable consequence of the reality of external objects (bāhyārthatā) would follow.

If it is argued that it is by its very nature (*prakṛti*) such that it is precisely that [nature] which constitutes affliction (*kliṣṭatā*), then, since there is neither decrease nor increase [in that nature], consider by what means liberation could be achieved. (HSvs 5.2.408)

If it is argued that even though no external object exists, this delusion characterized by the grasped and the grasper is our "afflicted state," like the error of seeing two moons; [then we reply: 5.2.409.
Let this be so; however, this [perception] must arise from a different cause distinct from that [cause], for the vision of two moons does not occur when the visual impairment (timira) is absent.
Nor is that cause merely non-existent, nor is it mere consciousness;
for if it were so, there would be a state of perpetual affliction, and thus liberation would not be possible. (HSvs 5.2.411)
If liberation does not exist, then surely every reflection is useless;
yet even if it does exist, one should always properly contemplate this very point.
Since the doctrine of consciousness-only is not established by reasoning in this way,
it is therefore not appropriate for a wise person to have an attachment even to this.
Sixth Fascicle (1): Momentariness is not established through causeless destruction.
As was previously stated in this very context regarding the proof of momentariness:
Because a cause for destruction is untenable, that [matter] is now examined.
If it is conceptualized that an entity might be either perishable or imperishable because of a cause,
then the claim that there is no connection with a cause of destruction is not logical.
Since that [destruction] is held to be perishable in dependence upon a cause,
just as your own cause is established as producing a specific result.
In that way, this very nature arises from its own cause alone;
having encountered a cooperative cause, it performs such an effect.
Furthermore, nothing at all is produced by that auxiliary cause, because it exists simultaneously [with the effect]; and thus this has been stated by you.
Whatever is considered a benefactor, an adversary, or a cooperative factor,
all such things exist in relation to a continuum (*prabandha*), and never at a single moment.
Even if there is no distinction produced in the cause by the auxiliary factors,
there is nevertheless a distinction in the effect, because it acquires an excellence brought about by them.
And if it does not have that as its intrinsic nature, then the production of that fruit is not tenable,
because it would result in the arising of a homogeneous moment, just like other moments of that same kind.

Furthermore, it is a misplaced partiality toward the reason; for since [the reason] is not required when there is dependence on something else, that which is called an "effect" has been stated in vain. (HSvs 6.1.422)
For that [reason] is also equal to this, as it accomplishes a distinguished result;
indeed, it has been demonstrated through logical principles by relying upon the cause of existence (bhāvahetu).
And thus, the consideration by the wise of destruction as something distinct from the object being destroyed is indeed futile in this context. (HSvs 6.1.424)
Furthermore, if destruction were causeless, the state of being a perpetrator would not be logical;
for in that case, no one would ever be killed by anyone anywhere.
If it is argued that he is the killer because he is the cause of a specific continuum [of suffering], that is not so; for a continuum cannot arise from such a cause. (HSvs 6.1.426)
Because it is merely conventional, the cessation and arising of a continuum do not exist, like a flower in the sky;
since those [cessation and arising] are not its true nature, how could there be a cause for its production?
Furthermore, that which produces a moment of a different nature is not a destroyer;
for even by its own nature, it would incur that status [of being a destroyer] because there is no distinction in its being a producer.
If it is conceived that there is a "slayer" because of defilement (*saṃkleśa*),
this is not so according to your own system, because even this [notion of a slayer] is not tenable.

Defilement is the production of qualities, and that does not arise from what is merely undefiled; nor does it arise from that which has another as its companion, because there is no excellence [in the cause] derived from that.
If it is argued that, having attained that [cause], it [the entity] becomes of that nature because its essence is such,
then surely there is no damage even to the position of destruction, provided that destruction occurs only upon encountering a cause of destruction.
But others, relying on the produced [effect] and with respect to its existence, nature, and so forth,
have thus stated that the producer is in every way causeless.
That which exists does not produce itself, because that would lead to the consequence of futility;
nor is it logical for anything else [to produce it], due to faults such as the impossibility of its arising.
Furthermore, others [hold that] because the existence of both and so forth is impossible due to contradiction and the like,
and because there is an absence of the effect in the presence of the cessation of itself and so forth.

Nor is there a contradiction with perception regarding the state of being a producer, because that [perception] is not established there by means of valid cognition; for according to that principle, it is only the conventional usage [of such a thing] that is negated.
In the absence of pride, even another person’s conventional usage is negated; likewise, let it be seen here that [the object] is the referent of the term and cognition "existent. (HSvs 6.1.436)
(2) The proof of momentariness through causal efficiency is not established;
that which is proclaimed regarding a momentary entity—that its capacity for causal efficiency [is proven] because it perishes immediately after arising—is illogical. (HSvs_6.2.437)
Since there are only two possibilities— either that [cognition] itself or something other than it performs the causal function (arthakriyā)—
it lacks efficacy with respect to reality, because that [reality] arises from something else.
It is not logical that [the body] sustains itself, because it perishes immediately after birth;
nor is it logical that it perishes [spontaneously], because its destruction arises from its own cause.
If [the cause and effect] were different, it would not be coherent to say that "the capacity of one thing lies in another";
therefore, this is simply the existence of something else, and it is not logical for that [capacity] to exist without a basis.

Since that which is non-existent does not arise even when another existent is present, if it is that very thing which exists in such a manner, how can it be said that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is unestablished? [HSvs_6.2.441]
That which is their "existence" is said to be their "activity," yet this is not tenable in any respect;
reflect on this, for it contradicts the nature of being both an agent and an enjoyer. (HSvs 6.2.442)
And it has been demonstrated that the past [word] has no capacity with respect to that [cognition];
nor is there any other worldly word-meaning here—thus, [the opponent's position] is illogical.
(3) The proof of momentariness is not established by the transformation of one form into another;
nor is transformation a cause for proving momentariness,
because even when there is constant change, such a state of being is still perceived.
Since there is neither a transition to another entity nor an absolute non-arrival [of the same],
transformation is established by valid cognition and is indeed accepted by the wise.
Regarding what is said here, we reply: "Impermanence is the state of not remaining in that same condition.
This very thing does not exist [as a single entity]; therefore, if there were any otherness, persistence would be certain.
"That very thing does not exist" and "that [thing] does not exist"—alas, this is contradictory! Furthermore, it would follow that it has a beginning.
Furthermore, it is observed that the destruction of milk results in curd itself, which is imbued with the essence of the cow's milk;
however, this is not the case for oil and other substances. Therefore, transformation is established as being accompanied by continuity.
The non-existent is never produced, nor does the existent ever become non-existent in any way whatsoever;
for [otherwise], there would be an over-extension due to the absence of causal capacity and the loss of the nature of existence.
Therefore, by this reasoning, that which is other than eternal is understood through its being of such a nature;
for it is correctly apprehended through transformation, aided by cognition.

(4) For one who maintains that destruction occurs only at the end, the proof of momentariness is not established; for it is never logical to prove the destruction of the first moment by means of the final moment of destruction, since that [final state] is the very nature of that [first moment]. HSvs_[6.4]451 // 451 //
If it were of the nature of destruction from the very beginning, how could there be a perception of it at the end?
This is due to the deception caused by the production of successively similar [moments], as has been stated.
Prior to the perception of destruction at the end, destruction is inferred at the beginning because it was not seen;
for its non-perception is due to its being obstructed by something similar.
This too is indeed unreal, because that which is similar is actually distinct;
if there is no apprehension of the difference, how can there be an apprehension of it [the universal], given that it has that [particular] as its very nature?

If it is argued that this [cognition] is restricted to that object because it does not apprehend its difference from others due to the non-apprehension of those others, then that [restriction] is equal for the other [cognition]; how then is there any comprehension?
Moreover, in the absence of a Tathāgata, this word is surely empty;
for, being restricted by its similarity [to other words], the non-apprehension of that [Tathāgata] follows from the apprehension of it.

Furthermore, if this [cognition] exists, one must necessarily accept a single, continuous cognition whose nature consists in the apprehension of many [objects]; since that is so, how can it be momentary?
Furthermore, in the systems of other [schools], an object is not apprehended by cognition;
for even in the absence of that [cognition], the object would still exist, and thus it could never [be established] as a reality.
Even when there is grasping, if the cognition perishes immediately after its arising, then how indeed can it know the momentariness of that [object]? (HSvs_6.4) 459.

Because that very thing has that as its intrinsic nature, and because it arises from itself alone—just like blue and so forth—it is not subject to doubt regarding its falsity, due to its conformity with that [nature]. (HSvs 6.4) 460.

Nor can it be established by one's own inference, because a distinction in properties is impossible; for [the property to be proved] would transcend the nature of the logical mark (liṅga), and its essential nature and so forth would be untenable.
In this way, through reasoning, the connection of a permanent entity with causal efficiency is also not perceived;
for all cognition whatsoever is, without exception, momentary.
Likewise, because its nature is manifold, it is not the case that causal efficacy (arthakriyā) is untenable for an object;
indeed, by logical necessity, such efficacy manifests either successively or simultaneously.

(5) A possible specific intention behind the presentation of the doctrines of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*) and consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*): Others, however, declare as follows: "The Buddha stated that 'everything is indeed momentary' in order to eliminate attachment [to permanence], and not because it is so in reality. (HSvs 6.5, 464)
In this way, even the teaching of "consciousness-only" is for the sake of removing attachment to external objects;
it is taught by the Arhat depending upon certain disciples who require such instruction.
Nor is this even unreasonable, because the Buddha, the Great Sage,
like a skilled physician, does not speak of things that are unreal in substance unless it serves a purpose.
(6) Refutation of the Doctrine of Emptiness:
But others who consider themselves wise say that everything is indeed empty;
for no entity can be established by reasoning as being either permanent or impermanent.
Because there is no causal efficiency (arthakriyā) in what is permanent, due to the contradiction between succession and simultaneity;
and because even that which is impermanent lacks arising and ceasing, it never exists [as a real entity].

The notion of arising and passing away, as well as [the notions of] delusion, bliss, and so forth, should be understood as being like a maiden’s dream or like the notion of the birth of a son [to a barren woman]. (HSvs 6.6) 469
Regarding this, others also state: "In this case, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists for establishing reality in such a manner? Or is it indeed entirely empty? [HSvs_6.6] 470.

If emptiness is well-established as the reality, how can there be existence? For surely, [existence] would persist because of the very presence of that [reality]. Thus one should reflect correctly. (HSvs 6.6) 471
The establishment of reality would thus exist even without a means of valid cognition;
that it is not otherwise is clearly the handiwork of God.
If, having set aside the stated pride, one claims that this entity is empty of something other [than itself],
then surely the effort expended in establishing the emptiness of the object to be proven is in vain.
Furthermore, if that [non-emptiness] were also non-empty, then because of the multiplicity of disputants,
the undesirable consequence of an abundance of non-emptinesses would follow.
To whatever extent there is a measure [of things], and likewise whoever are the objects to be instructed, all of them indeed exist; thus, for those who are many, there is no emptiness.
And thus, even the doctrine of emptiness is observed by the knower of reality to have been taught with a specific intention, in accordance with those to be trained.
The Seventh Chapter (1): An Exposition of the Doctrine of Permanence and Impermanence as Accepted by the Jains.
Others, however, say: "The world, consisting of living beings (*jīva*) and non-living matter (*ajīva*), is indeed beginningless."
Those who have exerted effort in the study of the scriptures [assert that reality] is endowed with existence, origination, destruction, and persistence.
Seeking a jar, a crown, or gold, people undergo grief, joy, or indifference— each with its respective cause— during the states of destruction, arising, and persistence.
One who observes the milk-vow does not eat curd, nor does one who observes the curd-vow eat milk; one who observes the non-dairy vow eats neither. Therefore, reality consists of these three natures.
Regarding this, others also state: "For these three [properties] are mutually contradictory;
they can never, at any time, coexist in one and the same place."
Arising is the becoming of what was non-existent; destruction is its opposite; and persistence is that which is devoid of both.
How could these three exist simultaneously in one and the same place?
Regarding sorrow, joy, and indifference, and whatever means for them have been stated here—
that too is improper, since they are held to be caused by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, for the proponent of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvādin), certainty regarding anything is not at all tenable;
for that [cognition], when considered independently, is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) precisely because it is not a means of valid cognition.
Though transmigrating, he is not a transmigrator; though liberated, he is indeed not that [transmigrator].
Because of the existence of both those forms and their opposites, everything is entirely unstable.
They say: "The arising of the crown is not of the nature of the destruction of the jar, nor is it something other than the gold; thus, these three are not mutually contradictory."
Furthermore, arising and passing away do not fail to exist, because they are understood through the cognition of persistence;
however, there is no valid means of knowledge for the claim that their persistence exists in reality while those two [arising and passing away] are non-existent.
Nor is there an absence of stability, for that is understood without dispute;
and if this [cognition] were erroneous, there would be no understanding of non-erroneousness in the world.
Arising is the coming into being of what was non-existent, characterized by its own causes and other factors;
destruction is the opposite of that, occurring through the absence of such a process of perception.
Likewise, this permanence is also of a nature that serves as the substratum for both;
otherwise, how could those three not be absent simultaneously in a single place? (HSvs 7.1.489)

It is logical that these three exist in this manner at one and the same place and at one and the same time because they have distinct causes; if there were no such distinction, it would not be tenable.

And others, out of delusion, maintain that [the object] exists for a moment; yet, since there is the absence of even one of those [characteristics] in that which has the nature of existing for only a moment, its reality cannot be established therein.
If that [momentary existence] is intended as mere being (bhāvamātra), then it is thus without qualification;
for the nature of abiding for a moment does not exist without arising and perishing.
Thus, it is never the case that what has come into being remains exactly as it was;
nor is it a worldly notion that destruction is simply the non-existence of what once existed.
And that which is proclaimed as grief and so forth, having latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as its cause—that is untenable; for that [stream of consciousness], being manifold, is never without a basis.

Because a real entity would necessarily result in being either always present or otherwise, and because it is a single entity, the consequence of over-extension and so forth follows by necessity when that [otherness] exists. (HSvs 7.1.495)
Furthermore, that which is described as "pride is indeed pride" and the total lack of certainty regarding it is also not tenable, because it is based on an absolute [one-sided] premise.
If it is argued that "that [cognition] is indeed valid cognition," [we reply: it is neither perceptual nor inferential.
If that were indeed valid cognition, how could it exist in the absence of those two?

There is neither self-existence nor other-existence, because existence and non-existence are contradictory; this is due to the same logic as [the refutation of] self-existence and non-existence, yet it is not the case that it does not exist there at all.
If this is merely imagined and not so in reality, then what fault is there in that? There is none; however, it does not follow that its [imagined] nature actually exists.
Therefore, because the correct establishment of valid cognition is based precisely on non-absolutism (anekāntata),
the supreme certainty of the proponent of *syādvāda* is necessarily appropriate.
By this, that which was stated—that "everything [is explained]"—has been refuted.
Nevertheless, something else is said here for the sake of the student's further understanding.
If the transmigrating being is that very same [person], how can there be the possibility of liberation?
If the liberated one is also that very same [person], then the designation [of "liberated"] would be without foundation.
That which is called "liberated" because it is completely freed from saṃsāra—
this is not possible for that very [person] without its having attained that state.
And when that very thing exists in such a manner, the entity— consisting of both its cessation and its other state—
is established by the force of logic itself, like a substance and its modifications.
If even as a child one does not feel shame for the deeds of childhood,
and as a youth one does not feel shame for them either, then another person acts for the sake of the future through those very same deeds.
It is neither young nor even old, and its activity is not for the sake of another;
that entity consists of lineage and so forth, and its absence would otherwise occur.
Positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), designated as substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*),
constitute the reality (*vastu*) through their mutual pervasion, by virtue of existing as both difference and non-difference.

Mutual pervasion is not tenable in the case of absolute difference or absolute identity, because it would lead to over-extension, due to [the resulting] oneness, and because the relationship between word and object would be untenable. (HSvs 7.1.508)
When difference speaks of mutual exclusion and pervasion speaks of the opposite, then,
because both difference and non-difference exist, there is the possibility of their mutual pervasion.
Thus, in this matter which is not contradicted by reason, the raising of objections by people merely reveals either their addiction [to fault-finding] or their dullness of intellect. (HSvs 7.1.510)
Indeed, that contradiction which arises from logical principle (*nyāya*) is what is called "contradiction" here;
for [otherwise], such a contradiction would be unestablished in cases such as absolute difference between those two.
That clay substance which is not devoid of other properties such as being a lump and so forth,
or that which is separated from those [properties], is never perceived in its isolation anywhere.

Therefore, by that reasoning, it is non-existent; and because both [properties] are established as one, there is consequently a contradiction elsewhere, characterized by the consequence of the absence of that [property].
And since this [entity] consists of different classes [of properties], there is no fault such as infinite regress;
for [the properties] are restricted, and because distinct difference and so forth are impossible.
Since there exists neither non-difference devoid of difference, nor difference devoid of non-difference,
but only the absolute [reality], how can there be conceptual construction therein?
In whatever form there is a difference, is it that [form] alone, or both?
Because the solitary [part] is non-existent here, and because that which exists has already been explained.
And since that [object] is understood by means of valid cognition to possess both natures,
for this reason too it is merely a conceptual construction consisting of a genus and so forth, which leads to an infinite regress.
For in this way, even defects such as the two-fold fault do not constitute a refutation,
because difference and non-difference are established through their being correctly of a different genus (*jātyantara*).
By this, that which was stated by former masters— who, out of delusion, abandoned direct experience and followed the logic of "birth"— is refuted.
If substance and mode were different, a single entity could not possess both natures;
if they were non-different, consider how the presence or absence of either one could be possible.
When one thing does not cease upon the cessation of another,
the former is necessarily seen to be distinct from the latter, just as a white horse is distinct from a camel.
The mode ceases, but not the substance; therefore, that [mode] is not non-different from the substance.
For if there were no difference, there would be no cessation, just like the nature of the substance itself.
Moreover, the position that [the universal] is something entirely other than both difference and non-difference has already been rejected;
alas, such a thing would possess a nature that is a distinct category altogether from the conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference.

Furthermore, how could those defects—which are established as being absolutely distinct in terms of their genus—converge upon this [entity], which consists of a different genus? This is so whether there be difference, non-difference, or both. (HSvs 7.1.524)
Something necessarily ceases, and for that [cessation], there is likewise nothing else [that does not cease].
Therefore, it is precisely its differentiation [from others] that constitutes its cessation; otherwise, how could there be such things as cessation?
By the power of yoga, the notion that "it belongs to him" is sublated as being merely a distinction;
when it is said that "its location is non-different from his," it is expressed thus through a pervasive correspondence (*vyāpti*).
Therefore, the statement that "it is merely a distinction from that" is contrary to experience;
for since that very thing exists in such a state, it consists of both its own cessation and its opposite.
That which cannot be established without both persistence and cessation—
its very nature as such should be contemplated with subtle intelligence.
But since that very thing exists in such a state because it arises as such,
no fault whatsoever accrues to us.
And this observation, being accompanied by positive and negative concomitance, establishes the existence of a thing in such a way because that thing has that very nature. (HSvs_7.1.530)
Moreover, even difference does not constitute a refutation for that proponent of non-absolutism (anekāntavādin),
because he maintains that a real entity consists of a nature comprising different classes (jātyantara) and is thus both eternal and non-eternal.
And this is determined to be so by the force of recognition;
for on this earth, the notion "this is that very same thing" is already established in the world.

Furthermore, it is not tenable according to sound reasoning that there is a transformation [of the Tathāgata], because the Tathāgata is understood to be without distinction of entity despite differences in time and so forth. (HSvs 7.1.533)
If there were absolute identity, there would be no plurality; and if there were plurality, this [reality] could not be one.
Therefore, how indeed could it possess that nature? Thus, it must consist of both these aspects.
But when that very [cognition] exists in such a state through some connection with differentiation,
it is also appropriate for the cognizer to possess that state in its primary sense.
Because it is eternally one and conjoined [with its substratum], this [universal] is not logically consistent even when there is a difference between individuals;
for, by the consequence that "it is here," it would follow that "this is that very same thing," which is untenable.
It is logical [to posit an external object] based on the non-cognition of similarity, and not even by the force of error;
for if these two [the object and its cognition] are not apprehended, the postulation of similarity is not tenable.
And even though it is erroneous, it is never sublated by reality;
furthermore, there is no proof whatsoever for the existence of such yogic cognition.

Various yogis perceive [reality] as manifold; yet there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramā*) for the claim that it is not manifold, because the teaching proceeds in accordance with the needs of those to be trained (*vineya*).

And that [cognition] which is observed with respect to nails, hair, grass, and so forth, when they have been cut and grown back again— that too is a mere semblance of that [perception], for it is not that very [perception] itself.
For just as perception is not invalid even when it has the appearance of being so,
so too should this [inference] be understood as a valid means of knowledge.
Since this [objection] is not undesirable because it is a conceptualization of sensory cognition (mati-jñāna),
it follows by the force of this very point that the permanence, impermanence, and so forth of an entity are established.
The Eighth Chapter (1): Refutation of the Doctrine of Non-dual Brahman (Advaita).
Others, however, desire non-duality by means of the absorption of [the distinctions between] Being, Brahman, and so forth.
For that which differentiates existence is nothing other than that very [consciousness] itself.
Just as a person afflicted by cataracts perceives the pure sky as if it were filled with various distinct particles, so too does one falsely imagine [the mind].
In the same way, this stainless Brahman, free from conceptual construction, appears as if it has attained impurity and manifests in the form of differentiation due to ignorance.
Regarding this, others say as follows: ignorance is not distinct from existence;
it is that very same thing, and thus the appearance of difference is without foundation.
That very [consciousness], although its nature is non-differentiation, is the basis for the appearance of differentiation;
this cannot be understood without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, even if the means of valid cognition exists, since it is distinct from the object of cognition, non-duality itself does not exist; therefore, in the absence of that [means], [non-duality] would lack a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, due to the distinction between knowledge and ignorance, it is sublated by that very independent [means of valid cognition];
likewise, because of its connection with doubt and so forth, let it be reflected upon through dependent origination.
Others explain it thus for the sake of establishing equanimity:
"The teaching of non-duality is indicated in the treatise, but not as the ultimate reality. [HSvs 8.1.550]
And this is not contradicted by reasoning, because of the established status of the true scriptures and so forth,
and because of the existence of saṃsāra and liberation, as well as the accomplishment of effort for that purpose.
Otherwise, if non-duality were the ultimate reality, alas, the futility of all religious practice would follow as an undesirable consequence for both saṃsāra and liberation.
Others,
moreover, speak thus: there is no such thing as liberation at all, nor is there any possibility of it, nor any means for its attainment.
Or why is it that, due to the absence of means, this does not always occur for all embodied beings?
If that [transformation] depends upon the transformation of karma and so forth,
then why is it that the transformation of karma and so forth is likewise [dependent], given its beginninglessness?
Because that very [consciousness] possesses a variegated nature, it is not tenable to say "it is thus," since its superior state is indeed said to have arisen many times.
Regarding this as well, others describe that there exists a supreme means for the reality of liberation, consisting of vision and so forth, which was spoken by the Omniscient One.
Vision, the seed of liberation, rightness, the knowledge of reality, the end of suffering, and the beginning of happiness—these are proclaimed as its synonyms. (HSvs 9.1.557)
Because the state of being capable from beginningless time is conjoined with that very nature,
it is likewise fully established even when the most excellent and other such karmic states have passed away.
Only a rare individual, having pierced through the most formidable knot of karma by means of virtuous disposition, attains that vision.
And when this [knowledge] exists, that fortunate person, endowed with right vision and whose soul is purified by faith in the truth, does not delight in the ocean of existence.
He perceives its form as it truly is with the eye of intelligence,
according to the correct treatises, like one whose eye disease has been destroyed.
Having seen that, he reflects thus with a tranquil inner self,
relying upon a supreme sense of spiritual urgency that is grounded in the true nature of things as they are.
Afflicted by birth, death, old age, disease, illness, sorrow, and other such calamities—a terrible great ocean that serves only to torment men! Alas! (HSvs 9.1.563)
But liberation is for the sake of supreme happiness; it is free from the afflictions of birth and so forth, liberated from the power of fear, and forever devoid of all harm.

Violence and the like are the cause of existence, because one observes their connection with suffering and so forth; conversely, non-violence and the like lead to liberation, because they entail the cessation of affliction.
Having thus understood the worthlessness of worldly existence and the virtuous nature of liberation,
the one of purified self constantly strives for that goal in accordance with the scriptures.
He performs a difficult task for base beings,
because of his firm attachment to liberation, like a lover within a brothel.
If the practice does not properly accomplish a specific goal that is to be attained,
it causes mental distress because of the obstruction to the realization of that state.

And therefore, when that [which is commonly called difficult] is not properly examined, it is seen that something else is truly difficult by right principle: namely, that which accomplishes the abandonment of the objects to be discarded.
Just as a wise man afflicted by disease, tasting even a slight measure of health, proceeds with right joy toward the treatment despite its difficulty, so does the Buddha.
In the same way, the best of men should be understood as being seized by the disease of saṃsāra;
having attained even a small measure of the health of tranquility, he applies himself to its remedy with sincere devotion.
And thus proceeding according to his capacity with a firm resolve,
having attained pure conduct, he gradually obtains absolute knowledge.
Then, having become all-knowing and having brought about the destruction of the karma that sustains existence through the yoga of knowledge, he attains eternal liberation.
Regarding that which was stated at the beginning— "the yoga of knowledge is pure austerity," and so forth—
the intended meaning of its essential purport is now being declared.
The lords of yogins have proclaimed the supreme pinnacle of the yoga of knowledge to be the stability known as *śaileśī*; from that, liberation follows without a doubt.
It consists of dharmas because it has the nature of one's own dharma; it bestows liberation because it is a means for purification;
it is inexhaustible because it does not fall away, remaining thus forever in liberation.
There is no complete cessation of the transformation of conduct,
because it is stated in the scripture that the perfected one (siddha) is neither a practitioner of conduct nor anything other than that.
Furthermore, its cessation here cannot logically result from the cessation of its state,
just as when a time limit has expired, the established nature of that thing indeed persists.
Therefore, it is correctly established that liberation comes from the yoga of knowledge;
thus, there is no fault in this being sung in accordance with other tantras.
The Tenth Chapter (1): A Refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka’s Refutation of Omniscience.
Regarding this, others assert: "An omniscient being does not exist at all."
"Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it," so say those who follow the *Nyāya*.
The omniscient one is not apprehended by the means of valid cognition that is direct perception;
nor is there any concomitant mark (liṅga) that is invariably connected with him.
Nor can it be established by scripture, since that [scripture] which propounds injunctions and the like is not itself perceived; nor can it be understood through analogy.
Not even by presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) can every object be established, for that [object] is possible even without it;
since the five means of valid cognition do not apply there, non-existence (abhāva) is the means of valid cognition in that case.
The establishment of dharma and adharma, it is said, arises from the scripture known as the Veda;
for that [Veda] is authorless and therefore free from defects caused by a [human] author.
And it has been said: "Since the Veda, like light, is common to all, for what purpose is a man postulated as the knower of dharma and adharma? (HSvs 10.1.585)
From this [consciousness], the distinction between sacrificial rites (*iṣṭa*) and charitable works (*pūrta*), which is established in all the worlds,
arises solely through the conventional establishment of linguistic usage, just like the [distinctions of] days and so forth.
That which is given within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi) by officiating priests through the consecration of mantras in the presence of Brahmins is designated as *iṣṭa*.
Tanks, wells, rest-houses, and temples,
as well as the gift of food— this is designated as *pūrta*.
Therefore, that virtuous conduct of the dispassionate Great Being—
which consists of meditation and so forth, and which yields the fruit of liberation— is declared to be the highest good.
For even the entire system of the castes and stages of life originates from that [Veda];
since he is the seer of objects beyond the senses, there is no other purpose for it whatsoever.
Regarding this, some proponents of omniscience say:
"How can the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition be established in that case? (HSvs 10.1.591)

If that perception were to have all objects as its domain and thus act as a negator [of non-existence], how could there be non-existence? If you say it is not so, then this [objection] applies equally here as well.
Furthermore, phenomena and so forth are also perceptible because they are objects of cognition, just like a jar and the like;
since everything is such for someone, there is no [such thing as] non-inferential knowledge.
Its establishment is also derived from scripture, since this [dharma] is the fruit of the Vedic injunction;
and its validity is intrinsic, as is its eternity, just like that of the Veda itself.
Because all doubts residing in the heart are resolved by grasping that [object], there is no further need for comparison when that [object] is grasped; nor is it otherwise in other cases either.
The cognition of supersensible objects through scripture is also understood by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);
otherwise, a lack of confidence would arise in that regard for one who is still subject to cognitive obscurations (*chadmastha*).
Thus, it is not logical that there is simply a non-operation of the five means of valid cognition in that case;
nevertheless, to claim that "non-existence" is a means of valid cognition is merely the manifestation of blindness.
Alas! Even the establishment of dharma and so forth from the Veda proceeds correctly only by setting aside one who perceives supersensible objects;
how can this be? Let this be reflected upon.
It is not [established] by the tradition of the elders, because that [tradition] is characterized by having its root severed;
nor is its supersensuous object determined by one of limited vision.
The validity of a tradition regarding the nature of form is not logical;
let it be examined here as well, just like that of those who have been blind since birth.
The identity of that [transcendental] object with a worldly object cannot be determined,
except through the observation of its opposite.
Because it is eternal and not of human origin, whatever [scripture] contains that is non-worldly,
the suspicion of a wise person regarding that [scripture], as well as others, does not cease on this account.
And there is no means for its cessation except for one who perceives that which is beyond the senses;
and having established this, Dharmakīrti has rightly proclaimed this.
One who possesses passion and other defects does not understand the meaning of the Veda by himself, nor from another;
the Veda itself does not make it known—how then can there be any comprehension of the Veda’s meaning?
Regarding the Vedic revelation, "One who desires heaven should offer the Agnihotra," what is the authority for the claim that its meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat"?
If it is argued that, like a lamp and so forth, that word which illuminates its object is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by itself, then there is nothing [to be proven] in this case either.
Furthermore, a distorted manifestation certainly occurs in some cases;
for instance, a lamp makes the blue lotus appear red.
Therefore, cognition does not arise without distinction;
it is illogical to claim that [cognition occurs] "by itself" when it is dependent upon convention (*saṅketa*).
The convention as to whether [an object] is real or not does not eliminate doubt,
because of the perception of its various forms and due to one's own persistent attachment to one's own mental dispositions.

Even an explanation [of grammar] is not tenable because there is no means of valid cognition for [the Veda] being authorless, and because its correctness and so forth cannot be ascertained due to mutual contradictions. (HSvs 10.1.610)
The determination of its validity does not arise from corroboration by another means of knowledge;
for that [corroboration] is not tenable regarding what is beyond the senses, because it would contradict the very nature of such things.
Therefore, this explanation of his is a communication of his own intention;
it is not at all equal to the statement of Jaimini and others, nor to any other speech of yours.
In this world, one person says, "This is a post; this is the path," while another says, "I myself am saying it. Let the difference between these two be examined.
Nor can it be logically established that this [Veda] is not of human origin;
for in the absence of the activity of a speaker, those sounds would not be perceived.
